claims.text: A framework combining machine-learned interatomic potentials with advanced sampling can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across HEA compositional space.
High-entropy alloys in as-cast or thermally processed solid states exhibit complex multicomponent disorder.
Machine-learned potentials combined with advanced free-energy sampling can trace the entire solid-liquid coexistence region.
The protocol is applicable to HEAs containing at least five principal elements.
The protocol can operate under near-equilibrium or controlled non-equilibrium high-temperature melting conditions.
Relevant HEA configurations must be represented in the training and validation of the machine-learned potentials.
The free-energy landscape governs solid-liquid phase coexistence during melting.
Evolution of the solid-liquid interface captures local atomic rearrangements and latent-heat signatures.
Machine-learned potentials can accurately capture the complex interatomic interactions in HEAs.
Metadynamics or nested sampling can efficiently explore the rugged free-energy landscape relevant to HEA melting.
Computed free-energy differences allow precise determination of latent heat.
Following phase-boundary evolution allows precise determination of the volume change at melting.
The framework will predict melting points, latent heats, and melting volume changes within an error margin competitive with high-fidelity calorimetry.
The framework will achieve higher throughput than conventional DSC and traditional molecular dynamics.
The framework will consistently reproduce sharp phase-coexistence and latent-heat signatures across varying HEA compositions.
Conventional DSC and molecular dynamics using standard interatomic potentials are less efficient and may fail to capture the full configurational complexity of HEAs.
Accuracy and applicability depend on the transferability of the machine-learned potential, and alloys outside its training range may show larger deviations.
The approach may improve accuracy by approximately 10–20% over traditional methods, although the improvement is uncertain.
Experimental DSC, calorimetry, and in situ X-ray or neutron scattering can be used to validate the predicted melting and fusion properties.
Consistent deviations exceeding approximately ±10% across multiple compositions, together with failure to reproduce phase-coexistence and latent-heat signatures, would refute the framework.
